h1: Car shipping cost from New York: what actually sets the price
heroSub: Typical open and enclosed price bands from the NYC metro to ten destinations, the eight factors that move the number, the surcharges to expect, and how to tell a real quote from a bait price.
intro:
Car shipping cost is the first thing people ask about and the thing most websites explain worst. The honest answer: a running mid-size sedan on an open carrier from the New York metro costs roughly $550 to $800 to the Southeast and Midwest, $1,000 to $1,200 to Texas and Colorado, and $1,350 to $1,550 to the West Coast, booked about a week out in a normal month. Enclosed adds 30 to 50 percent. The rest of this page explains why your number lands where it does inside those bands.

Big Apple Car Shipping dispatches from ten New York offices, Buffalo to Brookhaven, and prices every load against what carriers are accepting on that lane this week. The quote tool beside the headline gives you a number now. If you want to understand how much it costs to ship a car from New York and why, keep reading.

sections.h2: The eight things that move a car shipping cost, in order of weight
sections.html:
Carriers price a load like a cab fare: how far, how easy, and how badly they want to go there. Heaviest first:

  • Distance. The biggest single input. A 225-mile run to Washington, D.C. and a 2,790-mile run to Los Angeles are different jobs, but not twelve times different, as the next section explains.
  • Route popularity and lane balance. New York to Florida is a busy lane with trucks heading both ways, so rates stay sane. New York to Montana is not. A driver who deadheads home empty charges for the empty miles.
  • Vehicle size and weight. An open hauler carries eight to ten cars within a strict axle weight limit. A Tahoe takes the space and weight of a sedan and a half, so it pays more.
  • Running or not. A car that starts, steers, and brakes drives up the ramp in three minutes. One that does not needs a winch and a willing driver.
  • Open vs enclosed. Enclosed trailers carry fewer cars, cost more to run, and are scarcer, so the premium is real.
  • Season. January through March southbound, June through August everywhere, and holiday weeks all push rates up.
  • Pickup and delivery flexibility. A three-day window and a meeting point near a highway let dispatch pick a cheaper truck. One fixed date on a tight Brooklyn side street does not.
  • Fuel prices. Diesel is a carrier's largest variable expense. When it jumps 50 cents, long-haul rates follow within weeks.

sections.h2: Cost per mile: why longer trips are cheaper per mile
sections.html:
Short hauls are expensive per mile because loading, unloading, paperwork, and city traffic cost the same whether the car goes 200 miles or 2,000. From the NYC metro, runs under 300 miles typically price at $1.00 to $1.50 per mile, so Boston or D.C. lands around $300 to $400. Around 1,000 miles the rate settles near $0.70 per mile. Cross-country, a full truck rolling on interstates for four days, drops to $0.45 to $0.55 per mile.

That curve is why Florida at roughly 1,100 miles and California at roughly 2,800 miles are only about double each other in price.

sections.h2: Typical car shipping cost from New York by destination
sections.html:
The table below gives typical bands for a running mid-size sedan booked about a week out, with enclosed at a 30 to 50 percent premium. Pickups for these lanes leave from our Bronx, Yonkers, and Long Island offices most days. Our New York to Florida car shipping guide breaks our busiest lane down by city.

Add $100 to $250 for an SUV or pickup, and expect the top of each band in peak months. These are the ranges loads actually move at, not promises, because the rate a carrier accepts on Tuesday can differ from Friday.

Surcharges are not padding. Each maps to carrier space, time, or risk. Typical adds on top of the base open rate:

  • SUV, minivan, or pickup: $100 to $250 for the extra length and weight.
  • Dually or long-bed truck: $200 to $400, because it takes a slot meant for two cars or must ride a flatbed.
  • Inoperable vehicle: $100 to $200 for the winch, if the car still rolls, steers, and brakes. One that does none of those needs a forklift and prices case by case.
  • Enclosed carrier: 30 to 50 percent over open. Our enclosed auto transport page covers when it is worth it.
  • Expedited pickup: $150 to $300 for a truck in 24 to 48 hours instead of the normal window.
  • Mountain, island, or remote delivery: $100 to $300, or a terminal handoff, where a 75-foot rig cannot reach.
  • Oversized or lifted: $150 to $500 by height; over roughly 7 feet may not clear a two-deck trailer at all.
  • Extra items in the car: usually free up to about 100 pounds in the trunk, then $50 to $150; a full cabin can be refused.

sections.h2: How instant quotes work, and why the lowest one is usually bait
sections.html:
Nearly every auto transport company you reach online is a broker, including us, and brokers do not own trucks. We post your load to a national dispatch board where licensed carriers see the route, the car, the dates, and the price offered, and a driver accepts it if the money works for his route. An instant quote is a broker's estimate of what gets a carrier to click accept this week, plus the broker's fee.

If four quotes come in at $900 to $1,000 and one comes in at $600, the $600 quote is not a better deal. It is a load that will sit on the board unaccepted because no driver will take it at that number. The usual outcome is a call near your date saying the rate needs to go up, or no truck at all. Auto transport prices in NYC are set by carriers, not by whoever has the boldest website. A quote well under the pack is a bait price, and it will not move until it is raised to market.

sections.h2: Deposit, balance, payment methods, and what is included
sections.html:
The standard structure is a deposit at booking, charged when a carrier is assigned, and the balance paid to the driver at delivery. Most drivers take cash, Zelle, or a cashier's check; some accept cards with a processing fee and some do not. Policies vary by carrier, so we confirm the accepted methods when your truck is assigned.

A quoted price from us is the price: no fuel surcharges later, no insurance fees, no taxes bolted on at delivery. The number includes door-to-door pickup and delivery where the truck can safely reach, the carrier's cargo insurance for the vehicle while it is on the trailer, and any applicable taxes. It does not cover personal belongings, which carrier insurance excludes, or a job that changes after booking, like a car that will not start. Our car shipping checklist covers how to avoid those surprises.

sections.h2: Seasonal calendar and honest ways to save
sections.html:
January through March, southbound rates climb as snowbirds head for Florida and Arizona; the return wave runs April into May. June through August is peak on every lane as family moves and military orders stack up. Thanksgiving and late December are tight because drivers go home. The cheapest months from New York are typically late September through early December, plus mid-March for northbound loads when trucks return empty from Florida. Our snowbird car shipping page has the Florida calendar in detail.

The ways to save that actually work: give dispatch a pickup window of three to five days, offer to meet the truck at a large lot near a highway instead of a tight residential block, choose an open carrier unless the car genuinely needs enclosed, book two to three weeks ahead so you are not competing for the last truck, and ship the car running with a quarter tank of fuel.

When cheaper is not better: if you need the car by a fixed date, pay for expedited car shipping rather than hoping a low-priced load gets picked up. If the vehicle is worth more than typical cargo coverage, the enclosed premium is cheaper than an uncovered loss. And if one quote is far below the others, treat it as a delay you have not been told about yet.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to ship a car from New York to Florida?
faqs.a: A running sedan on an open carrier typically costs $650 to $750 from the NYC metro to Florida, booked about a week out in a normal month. SUVs and pickups add $100 to $250, enclosed adds 30 to 50 percent, and January through March rates sit at or above the top of the band as snowbird demand peaks.

faqs.q: Why did my instant quote change after I booked?
faqs.a: A real quote should not change unless the job changes, for example a car that will not start or an address the truck cannot reach. If a company quoted far below market and then asked for more money close to your date, that was a bait price no carrier would accept. Compare quotes against the pack, not the lowest one.

faqs.q: Is the deposit refundable if no carrier is assigned?
faqs.a: Our deposit is charged only when a carrier is assigned to your load, so if we cannot place your car there is nothing to refund. If you cancel after a truck is assigned, the deposit covers the dispatch work already done. Ask any company to put deposit timing and cancellation terms in writing before you book.

faqs.q: Does the price include insurance and taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The quoted price includes door-to-door service, the carrier's cargo insurance for your vehicle while it is on the trailer, and any applicable taxes. It does not cover personal items left inside the car, which carrier insurance excludes. Ask for the carrier's insurance certificate once your truck is assigned.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to ship an inoperable car than to fix it first?
faqs.a: Usually not. An inoperable surcharge runs $100 to $200 if the car rolls, steers, and brakes, and more if it needs a forklift. A dead battery or a flat tire fixed for under $150 before pickup is almost always cheaper than the surcharge, and it widens the pool of carriers willing to take it.
